::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

info.title: How Many Sites, Participants, and Trials? A Tutorial on Multilevel Power Analysis for Multisite Studies with Repeated Measures

author.affiliation:
Departamento de Psicología Básica

Departamento de Psicología Básica I
								Universidad Nacional de Educación a Distancia

text.text: Multisite collaborations are increasingly common in psychological science.
Planning a multisite study with repeated measures involves more than deciding how many participants to recruit.
Researchers must also determine how many sites to include and how many observations to collect from each participant.
These decisions become particularly challenging when the experimental effect may vary across both participants and sites.
Unfortunately, most widely used power analysis tools do not accommodate the complexity of these structures.
In this tutorial, we provide a practical introduction to multilevel power analysis for three-level multisite studies.
We first discuss how to identify and model the effect of interest, accounting for different sources of heterogeneity and the population to which researchers intend to generalize their findings.

We then demonstrate how to estimate statistical power through simulation using {simr} and how to optimize the number of trials, participants, and sites using {mlpwr}, considering their relative costs.

Finally, we illustrate how to explore alternative assumptions about effect size and between-site heterogeneity, verify the power of the selected architecture, assess estimation precision, and calculate the minimum detectable effect size.
The accompanying R code provides an adaptable workflow to help researchers plan multisite studies that balance their inferential goals with their available resources.
Multisite collaborations are becoming increasingly common in psychological science.
Perhaps you are considering coordinating one yourself.
Brave choice!
One of the keys to success will be careful planning.
You might think that achieving sufficient statistical power is simply a matter of recruiting enough participants.
However, in a multisite study with repeated measures, power also depends on how many sites you include and how many observations you collect from each participant.
To refer to these decisions collectively, we will use the term study architecture.
Since multisite architectures are by definition hierarchical, multilevel models (also known as hierarchical or mixed-effects models) are a natural choice for analyzing these datasets.
We assume basic familiarity with these models1 and R, but no prior experience with simulation-based power analysis or {simr} (Green & MacLeod, 2016) and {mlpwr} (Zimmer et al., 2024) is needed.

text.text: You might not have heard the term "study architecture" before2.
We use it to refer to the hierarchy of levels in the data and the number of units at each level (i.e., the level sizes).

For instance, the multisite study we will use throughout this tutorial has three levels: the experimental task consists of 32 trials (Level 1) completed by each of 16 participants (Level 2) at each of 12 sites (Level 3).

The hierarchy is therefore trials ⊂ participants ⊂ sites, and this particular architecture has a trial size of 32, a participant size of 16, and a site size of 12; in total, (32×16×12) 6,144 observations.

trials_size <-32 partis_size <-16 sites_size <-12 # Generate all combinations of trials, participants, and sites (6,144 rows) architecture <-expand.grid(trial = 1:trials_size, participant = factor(1:partis_size), site = factor(1:sites_size))

text.text: Before thinking about power, you first need to decide which effect you want to estimate.

Imagine your main research question concerns the effect of an experimental condition that varies from trial to trial within participants (such as the Stroop effect, which is the response time difference between congruent and incongruent trial conditions), hereafter coded as -0.5 and 0.5, respectively: # Predictor (independent variable or factor): "condition" condition_pattern <-rep(c(-0.5, 0.5), length.out = trials_size) # Add the condition variable to the architecture design architecture$condition <-rep(condition_pattern, times = partis_size * sites_size)

text.text: You want to know whether condition affects participants' response (e.g., response times).
For the moment, let's ignore the hierarchical structure of your data-trials nested within participants-and start with the simplest possible model:
The coefficient for condition (i.e., the fixed slope) is your estimand: the average experimental effect you want to estimate.
If the effect is as large as you expect, you want your study to have a good 2We introduce the term "study architecture" because other commonly used terms can be ambiguous in this context.
We avoided the term "sample", because one could reasonably argue that the 12 sites themselves constitute a sample of sites, just as the trials could be regarded as sampled units.
Also, in multisite research, the term sample is also commonly used to refer to the participant sample contributed by each site.

Similarly, we avoided using "study design", because design is already widely used to describe how independent variables are manipulated or how an experimental task or procedure is structured. chance of detecting it.
Let's say, an 80% chance (i.e., 80% power).
However, the model used to capture this estimand is currently too simplistic, because it assumes that the effect will be identical across participants and sites.
Let's refine it little by little by accounting for different sources of heterogeneity in the data.
Of course, participants are unlikely to respond identically.
Some may generally produce higher (or lower) responses than others, regardless of condition.
You can represent this variation by adding a participant-level random intercept:
This allows each participant to have their own average response level.
But participants may also differ in the size of the experimental effect itself.
Some participants may be very sensitive to condition, others not at all, and some may even show an effect in the opposite direction.

Such heterogeneity is common in psychological research, so unless there are strong reasons to assume otherwise, you should allow the effect of condition to vary across participants by adding a participant-level random slope:
This allows each participant to have their own average response level (the term 1) and their own experimental effect (the term condition).
In addition, the model estimates the covariance between both terms3.

In a multisite study, the same logic applies to between-site heterogeneity, as experimental effects have been shown to vary across sites in previous multisite collaborations (e.g., Klein et al., 2018).

text.text: From this point on, we will make the hierarchical structure explicit by writing participants as nested within sites: site:participant.
This is essential when participant identifiers are repeated across sites (e.g., "P001", "P002"), because the model must distinguish "P001" at one site from "P001" at another.
If participant identifiers are already unique across the entire dataset (e.g., "S1_P001", "S2_P001"), using participant alone would be equivalent.
Still, the nested notation makes the threelevel structure more transparent.
First, could sites differ in their average response levels?
If so, you can add a site-level random intercept: 3For instance, participants with higher mean performance might also be the ones who show larger experimental effects.
You can set this covariance to zero using || instead of |.
This accounts for the possibility that some laboratories systematically produce higher or lower response values than others.
More relevant for many multisite studies, you should also ask whether the experimental effect itself could differ across sites.
Perhaps the manipulation works more strongly in some laboratories than in others because of differences in recruitment, implementation, language, equipment, or other contextual factors.
If you want your model to represent this possibility, you need a site-level random slope:
Now the model allows both participants and sites to differ not only in their average responses, but also in the size of the condition effect.
In this first example, the estimand is a trial-level effect, because condition varies across trials within participants.
Similarly, you might instead be interested in a participant-level effect, such as the effect of gender, which varies across participants within sites.
The model for this estimand would therefore be:
Here, the fixed effect of gender is the estimand: the average difference in response associated with gender.
Note that gender is not included in the participant-level random-effects structure because it does not vary within participants.
Therefore, you should not include a participant-level random slope for gender.
However, because gender does vary across participants within sites, its effect can itself vary across sites.
The site-level random slope for gender allows the model to represent this betweensite heterogeneity.
So far, we have only considered the main effects of condition and gender.
However, with multiple predictors, you may also be interested in whether their effects interact.
For example, does the effect of condition differ across participants depending on their gender?

If this interaction is your primary research interest, then your estimand would be the interaction between condition and gender, also known as a cross-level interaction: response ~ condition * gender + (1 + condition | site:participant) + (1 + condition * gender | site)
Here, the fixed effect of condition:gender would be your estimand: how much the average effect of condition changes across levels of gender.
Again, because gender does not vary within participants, neither gender nor the condition×gender interaction can have a participant-level random slope.
However, both can vary across sites, because sites contain participants from different levels of gender and trials from different levels of condition.
The site-level random slope for condition*gender therefore allows the magnitude of this interaction to differ across sites.
And yes, your estimand could operate at an even higher level.
Imagine that your multisite study includes several sites from each of two countries, and you are interested in the average difference between countries:
Here, the fixed effect of country is the estimand: the average difference in response between the two countries.
Or you could model the interaction condition*country instead4, as in the previous example.
Because country does not vary within participants or within sites, it cannot have participant-level or site-level random slopes.
So far, all our estimands have been fixed effects, but heterogeneity itself could also be your target of inference.

For instance, you might also be interested in the between-sites heterogeneity itself, so your estimand becomes the variance of the site-level random intercepts or slopes (see Bloom et al., 2017; Xie & Kelcey, 2026).

text.text: Once you have identified your estimand, the next question is: to which population do you want to generalize it?
In a multisite study, this depends on whether participants and sites are treated as fixed or random effects.
Let's assume again that your estimand is the trial-level effect of condition.
Imagine that participants are treated as random, but the effect of condition is estimated separately for each of the particular site in your study:
The interaction condition*site allows the condition effect to differ across the recruited sites, but these site-specific effects are treated as fixed.
In other words, the model makes no assumption that these sites represent a broader population of sites.

Your inference can generalize across participants similar to those sampled within these sites, but the site-specific effects refer to the particular sites that participated in the study (not to any potential site).
This may be appropriate if those sites are themselves the units you care about (e.g., because something specific happened in those particular sites) or if you have recruited few sites.
However, 4In R syntax, condition*country models both the interaction and the main effects of condition and country.

If you'd prefer to model only the interaction, you can use condition:country instead. multisite studies often aim to make broader inferences: we would like the estimated effect to generalize not only to new participants, but also to new sites similar to those that were sampled.
To do that, the site-specific condition effects should instead be treated as random:
The same logic applies to participants.

Treating participant-specific effects as fixed restricts inference to the particular participants observed, whereas treating them as random allows the model to regard them as a sample from a broader participant population.
You might be asking then: if random effects allow broader generalization, why would anyone model these effects as fixed?
The reason is that broader generalization requires the model to acknowledge that the effect may genuinely vary across participants or sites.
Once this heterogeneity is modeled, the average fixed effect is estimated with greater uncertainty than under a model that treats the observed units as fixed (Barr et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Once this heterogeneity is modeled, the average fixed effect is estimated with greater uncertainty than under a model that treats the observed units as fixed <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Barr et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, detecting the estimand may require more information, that is, larger trial, participant, or site sizes.
Broader generalization therefore places stronger demands on the study architecture: you may need more trials, participants, and sites to detect the effect with sufficient power.
How actual multisite studies have modeled their architectures.
Multisite studies tend to have a natural trials ⊂ participants ⊂ sites hierarchy.

Some study architecture planning approaches explicitly represent this hierarchy and allow the experimental effect itself to vary across sites through site-level random slopes, for example, Adetula et al. (2026) or Coles et al. (2022); see also the pre-data Registered Report by Meltzoff et al. (2026).

text.text: Now that you have defined your preliminary architecture and identified your estimand, your next step is to estimate the power of this architecture to detect it.
You may be familiar with other standard power software, such as G*Power (Faul et al., 2007) or the R package {pwr} (Champely, 2020).

text.text: They are widely used to conduct power analyses for t-tests, ANOVAs, correlations, or linear regression models, and rely on closed-form analytical solutions.
Unfortunately, for a multilevel model like yours, such closed-form solutions do not exist.
Instead, you have to estimate power intercept and slope describe variation around these population-average coefficients.
The residual standard deviation describes variation not captured by the fixed and random effects.
You can obtain most of the values needed directly from the model fitted by {lme4}:

If the estimated intercept-slope covariance appears substantively relevant, consider an additional scenario retaining it.
Note that such scenario also requires updating the theta vector used by lme4::simulate.formula() in the optimization function, simply replacing V_parti is insufficient for that function.
For obvious reasons, a study conducted at one site cannot estimate the distribution of random intercepts and slopes across sites.
Therefore, it cannot identify sd_site_intercept or sd_site_condition.
When previous multisite data are unavailable, you should inform between-site heterogeneity by other sources.
One approach is to use estimates from comparable multisite or meta-analytic studies.
For example, Dong et al. (2021) selected standardized effect-heterogeneity variances of 0.05 and 0.15 based on the empirical distribution reported by Weiss et al. (2017).

text.text: In either case, these assumptions should be explicitly justified, and the implications of alternative values for the selected study architecture should be evaluated.

There is also a subtler limitation: the condition coefficient from one site estimates the effect at that site, not necessarily the average effect across the population of sites to which you hope to generalize.
Thus, although the pilot offers an informative starting value for beta_condition, it cannot by itself establish the multisite population-average effect.
The parameters recovered from pilot_model are estimates, potentially imprecise ones.
In particular, a small pilot may provide unstable estimates of the experimental effect and the variability of individual slopes; some random-effect variances may even be estimated at the boundary.
Copying these point estimates into a simulation does not account for their estimation uncertainty.
Nor does it guarantee that the pilot is representative of future participants or sites.
We therefore recommend treating pilot estimates as starting points for a range of plausible scenarios, not as definitive population values.
For instance, you could repeat the analyses with a smaller beta_condition, a larger sd_parti_condition, and alternative values of sd_site_condition.
The section "Explore alternative assumptions" shows how to carry out this exercise, including re-optimizing the architecture under more demanding scenarios.
Where uncertainty is substantial, confidence intervals, external evidence, or an explicit distribution over plausible parameters can help motivate those scenarios.

Since this is insufficient, you should increase the level sizes of your architecture.
But… by how much?
Should you increase the number of trials, participants, or sites?
Calculating power with powerSim() for every possible combination would be computationally expensive.
So, let's use {mlpwr} to find an optimal combination within a feasible architecture space.
You now know that your preliminary architecture provides insufficient power, so the next step is to consider how many units you could feasibly collect at each level.
Let's imagine that you could increase the task to a maximum of 48 trials, require up to 36 participants per site, and recruit up to 20 sites.
These limits define your architecture space: architecture_space <-list(trials_size = c(32, 48), partis_size = c(16, 36), sites_size = c(12, 20))

text.text: Instead of evaluating every possible combination, find.design() from {mlpwr} uses a surrogate model to search this space efficiently.
This function requires you to create a simfun and a costfun.
Let's see how:
The simfun should receive an architecture and return TRUE when the estimand is detected and FALSE otherwise.

Fortunately, everything required inside this function is essentially what we have already learnt in the previous sections: 6When running these simulations, you may encounter singular fits (boundary estimates) or convergence warnings, especially with few sites.
Singular fits occur when random-effect variances are estimated as close to zero or correlations between random effects approach -1 or 1.
Convergence warnings indicate difficulties estimating model parameters and resulting solutions might be inadequate.
Both problems may arise when the data provide insufficient information to estimate a complex random-effects structure.
If these problems occur in most replications, consider fixing to 0 the correlations between random effects (using || instead of |).
Alternatively, you could use a Bayesian model (e.g., with {brms}) to regularize parameter estimates, although this is computationally more expensive.
You can inspect the warnings using power_preliminary$warnings.
Occasional warnings are not necessarily concerning, but frequent estimation problems should be investigated before interpreting the power estimates.

text.text: With the current assumptions, the optimal architecture consists of 32 trials, 19 participants per site, and 17 sites, with predicted power close to the desired .80.
This is a nice example where everything goes well, but sometimes find.design() may warn you that "the predicted value consistently lies at the edge of the parameter space".
If that happens, it is worth checking whether the selected architecture reaches one of the boundaries of the architecture space you specified.
Two things might be going on.
If the predicted power is still below your desired level and the architecture lies at the upper boundary, you may need to increase the maximum level sizes.

Conversely, if the selected architecture lies at the lower boundary while already achieving sufficient power, your search space may simply be broader than necessary, and you could consider allowing even smaller, cheaper architectures.
In any case, if the optimization has not stabilized, you can also try increasing the number of evaluations.
Your selected architecture depends on the assumed model parameters.

You should therefore repeat the optimization under more demanding but plausible scenarios, such as smaller effect sizes or greater between-site heterogeneity, to assess how robust your selected architecture is.

This suggests that the architecture space needs to be expanded to accommodate more demanding scenarios.
A smaller effect size requires more information overall, whereas greater between-site heterogeneity particularly increases the need for additional sites.

text.text: If detecting the originally assumed effect with 80% power remains your goal, you should reconsider the selected architecture, for example, by repeating the optimization with more evaluations or expanding the architecture space, and reassess the resulting design.
For precision, you can examine the variability of the estimated effects (called empirical standard error) and the average width of their 95% confidence intervals8.
You can also calculate empirical coverage: the proportion of intervals containing the true effect used to generate the data (which should be close to 1-𝛼 under correct model specification).

# Assess precision and confidence interval coverage: t_critical <-stats::qt(0.975, df = dfs) ci_lower <-estimates -t_critical * ses ci_upper <-estimates + t_critical * ses precision_results <-data.frame( mean_estimate = mean(estimates, na.rm = TRUE), empirical_se = sd(estimates, na.rm = TRUE), mean_model_se = mean(ses, na.rm = TRUE), 8For consistency with our significance test, the confidence intervals use the t distribution with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom. mean_95CI_width = mean(ci_upper -ci_lower, na.rm = TRUE), empirical_coverage = mean( ci_lower <= beta_condition & ci_upper >= beta_condition, na.rm = TRUE)) precision_results #> mean_estimate empirical_se mean_model_se mean_95CI_width empirical_coverage #> 0.1484726 0.05359122 0.05116042 0.2162517 0.948

text.text: The empirical standard error is .054, the average confidence interval width is .216, and empirical coverage is 94.8%.
While coverage assesses the calibration of the confidence intervals, their width indicates how precisely you can estimate the effect.
Finally, you can calculate the minimum detectable effect size (MDES): the smallest true effect that your selected architecture can detect with the desired power, given your other model assumptions.
To approximate the MDES, you can progressively change the assumed effect size in increments of, let's say, .01 and recalculate power.
If your architecture already achieves the desired power, you should search for smaller effects; otherwise, search for larger ones.
In this example, the architecture achieves approximately 76% power for an effect of .15, and 83.5% for an effect of .16.
Its approximate MDES is therefore .16.
Because this search uses only 200 simulations per additional effect size, the result is preliminary.
More simulations, particularly around the estimated threshold, would be needed for a robust final assessment.
You have made it through one of the most technical parts of planning your multisite study.
Hopefully, you now have a clearer answer to our initial question: How many sites, participants, and trials?
Well, it depends!
As we have seen, the answer depends on what you want to estimate, the population you want to generalize to, your assumptions about the data, and, of course, your available resources.
There is no universally optimal architecture, but we hope this tutorial and its accompanying code will help you find one that works for your study.
Good luck with your multisite adventure!

We then repeat the steps b) to d) many times.
The proportion of simulated studies in which the null hypothesis is rejected is your estimated power.
But let's first perform each operation separately before automating the whole procedure.

Your model can be represented conceptually as: response = beta_intercept + beta_condition*condition + # fixed effects u_parti_intercept + u_parti_condition*condition + # parti random effects u_site_intercept + u_site_condition*condition + # site random effects epsilon # residual error # (*) The notation extends naturally to additional predictors Where beta states for fixed effects and u states for the specific random effects of participant (u_parti) and site (u_site).

The values of these parameters are assumed, so it is crucial that you justify them using prior evidence such as previous data, pilot or meta-analytic studies, plausible ranges… Let's present an example of how to do this using estimates from a previous single-site study: Start with a previous single-site study or pilot Suppose you have data from a previous experiment conducted at one site.
As in your multisite study, each participant completed repeated trials under two conditions, coded as -0.5 and 0.5, and the outcome response is continuous (e.g., response time).

text.text: Create the cost function Two architectures may achieve the same power but have substantially different costs: An architecture with 5 sites and 40 participants per site might achieve the same power as one with 20 sites with 10 participants each, but the latter could be considerably more expensive.
How much more expensive?
That's something that you can represent in your costfun.
For example: trial_cost <-1 # Each trial has a cost of 1 unit. parti_cost <-25 # Each participant has an extra cost of 25 units. site_cost <-1000 # Each site has an extra cost of 1000 units.
